subject: Communication
title: The Devil's Advocate: Arguing What You Don't Believe
description: One-minute skill: The Devil's Advocate: Arguing What You Don't Believe.

hook.text: The Catholic Church appointed a literal 'Devil's Advocate' to argue against sainthood candidates.

buildup.text: Playing devil's advocate means deliberately arguing the opposing position to test the strength of an idea or decision.

discovery.text: Research shows groups with a designated devil's advocate make better decisions — they consider more options and catch blind spots.

twist.text: The technique fails if people know it's just roleplay and don't take it seriously.

climax.text: The greatest thinkers argue against their own positions regularly.

punchline.text: Attack your own ideas before someone else does. You'll improve them either way.

quiz.question: Where did the term 'Devil's Advocate' originate?

details.summary: Playing devil's advocate means deliberately arguing a position you do not hold to test the strength of the opposing view. This technique originated in the Catholic Church, where a designated advocate would argue against sainthood to ensure only worthy candidates were selected.
details.whyItMatters: Devil's advocacy prevents groupthink and strengthens decisions. If your idea cannot survive a determined counter-argument, it is not ready for implementation.
takeaways: The role originated in Catholic sainthood proceedings
Arguing against your own position reveals its weaknesses
Teams that use devil's advocacy make better decisions

faq.question: How should devil's advocacy be used in team settings?
faq.answer: Assign the role formally so the person is granted permission to challenge without personal consequences. Rotate the role so no one becomes the permanent critic. Focus on questioning assumptions and evidence rather than generating negativity. Set clear time boundaries.

faq.question: Can devil's advocacy become counterproductive?
faq.answer: Yes, when it becomes performative rather than genuine. If the advocate does not put real effort into constructing the counter-argument, it provides false confidence. Research shows assigned devil's advocacy is less effective than genuine dissent in improving decisions.
